edge_types.meaning: A container includes an asset.
A composite asset, bundle, cluster, or workflow includes a member asset.
A workflow uses an asset as an ordered or named step.
A use/run/deployment instance instantiates one or more assets.
An asset explicitly references another.
An asset was derived from another.
A reviewed asset replaces an older asset.
Code or workflow implements a contract or design.
A document explains another asset.
A test evaluates another asset.
An asset requires another.
Assets have bounded semantic or structural similarity.
Assets are semantically similar under an approved embedding or semantic-similarity gate; deferred until privacy, provider, retention, and eval controls exist.
Assets appear to serve the same architecture role even if their content differs; candidate relationship requiring review.
Assets are reviewed or candidate variants that share a core but may serve different contexts.
Assets have the same exact content SHA-256. Provenance and role may still differ.
Assets share enough deterministic chunks or signatures to warrant duplicate/variant review.
Most deterministic shingles from the source asset appear inside the target asset; generated candidate only.
Assets have a generated delta record describing exact or near-duplicate differences.
Assets provide non-identical capabilities that combine usefully.
A provider capability addresses a declared need.
A missing condition prevents activation.
A state change may make a dormant asset relevant.
A lesson is grounded in an event or asset.
Repeated lessons suggest a reusable skill.
An asset is constrained by a governance surface.
A routing, chunking, or orchestration asset directs work to a target asset or path.
An asset appears to handle a structural form, document form, workflow form, or domain-specific case type.
An evaluation or route harness is paired with a gold, golden, expected-output, or reference set.
A workflow or evaluation system produces or depends on a human-review packet.
An exception, failure, feedback, or evaluation asset produces a candidate learning signal.
A candidate adaptation, promotion, or reuse path requires an explicit human review gate.
An archived asset appears to be a preserved variant of another asset. This is not a deletion or canonicalization instruction.
Assets appear duplicate-like by role, name, or structure but do not yet meet exact or near-duplicate evidence thresholds.
A delta review suggests one asset is stronger on a bounded dimension while preserving both variants.
Assets appear useful together as a higher-level composite workflow or system.
Assets appear risky to combine without extra boundary, security, or authority review.
An asset may contaminate a target workflow if treated as default truth or authority without review.
A supporting asset can guide, validate, or enrich another asset but cannot override that source asset's authority.
A workflow part appears to produce an output that can become an input to another workflow part. Generated candidate only unless declared or reviewed.
Workflow parts appear to fill a similar role and may be interchangeable in a bounded context. This is not variant lineage or a canonical-preference claim.
A workflow part appears to be a narrower or domain-specific version of a broader workflow part.
A workflow part appears to be a broader reusable form of a narrower or domain-specific workflow part.
A security, privacy, source-scope, or quality gate routes an input or asset out of default use until review.
A generated signal, failure, or lesson candidate was observed inside a worktree, temp repo, archive, or repository attempt.
Assets or paths repeatedly changed together in local git history or repeated attempts.
A failure-like signal appears earlier than a later stabilizer or corrective artifact.
A later artifact appears to address an earlier failure signal. Generated candidate only.
A test, schema, validator, review packet, or gate appears to stabilize a workflow or attempt.
A counterfactual lesson suggests one step should happen before another in similar contexts.
A lesson candidate is intended to apply only under the stated context.
A lesson candidate explicitly warns that it should not be applied under the stated context.
A lesson candidate may be harmful if stripped from its context or applied as a universal rule.
A candidate lesson was inferred from one or more worktree, temp, archive, or repository attempts.
Assets or family versions differ in behavior-relevant structured content after deterministic normalization.
A candidate semantic-evolution record suggests one version evolved from another. Requires provenance review before source-order claims.
Assets differ mainly by formatting, path, metadata, fixture propagation, or copy lineage rather than semantic behavior.
A copied, temp, archive, changelog, or variant asset is evidence for a higher-level family lineage.

rule: Every generated edge must retain method, evidence, confidence, and scan provenance.
